1.pericope_label: God sends Jacob back to Bethel, and he purges his household of idols

schools.summary: Gill sets the appearing in Jacob's distress after the slaughter of the Shechemites, when he did not know what course to steer for his own safety and his family's, and holds that God then spoke, whether in a dream, or by an impulse on the mind, or by an articulate voice — supposing that this may have been the Son of God in human form, since Jacob afterwards speaks of God as of another Person distinct from himself. Calvin makes the delay itself the lesson: God did not appear at once but suffered his servant to be tormented with grief and excessive cares, that he might learn patience, deferring the consolation to the hour of extreme necessity, so that whenever we read such a passage we should reflect that the providence of God watches for our salvation even when it most seems to sleep. He asks why God did not translate Jacob elsewhere by a miracle instead of speaking to him, and answers that it is the principal business of our life to depend upon the word of God. On the idols he traces the contagion to one source: Rachel did not draw her father from his superstition but followed him in his fault, and spread the poison through the whole house; and Jacob, not ignorant of the evil, was so far under his wife's influence that by connivance he cherished the plague — convicting himself in the very word, by calling them strange gods.

Henry counts seven or eight years since Jacob came into Canaan: God had performed his part of the bargain and given him more than bread to eat and raiment to put on, and Jacob had bought ground and built an altar at Shechem — yet Bethel was forgotten. Time is apt to wear out the sense of mercies, he says; it should not be so, but so it is. God had exercised him with a sore affliction in his family to bring the vow to mind, and when that failed came himself; for as many as God loves he will remind of neglected duties, by conscience or by providences, and though it is best not to defer a vow, better late than never. At the strange gods Henry is astonished — strange gods in Jacob's family, strange things indeed; could such a family, taught the good knowledge of the Lord, admit them, and could such a master connive at them? Doubtless this was his infirmity, since those that are good themselves cannot always have those about them so good as they should be.

Clarke reads the circumstance politically: what had lately been done made it unsafe for Jacob to stay at Shechem, and while he was reflecting on the horrible act of Simeon and Levi, God graciously appeared to him. Of the idols he says they were the gods of the foreigners, notes that Jacob's servants were all Syrians and addicted more or less to idolatry, and thinks them likelier to be images of silver or gold from the spoils of Shechem than the teraphim Rachel stole, which he has already taken for astrological tables. Wesley says with Henry that the command to dwell there meant Jacob was to bring his household, that they might join in his devotions.

Ellicott will not have the charge of forgetfulness. Forty-two years had elapsed since the vow was made, and it had not been forgotten; Bethel was the goal of the patriarch's journeyings, and the divine command only the outward authorisation of what his conscience already dictated. On that account, he says, we cannot believe Jacob had remained long at Shechem, nomads being leisurely in their movements and capable of a great effort only occasionally. On the idols he gathers three sources at once — Rachel's teraphim, the gods brought from Haran, and the deities of the captive Shechemites — and makes the object of the reformation not merely the raising of Jacob's family but the initiating of the heathen in their households into the true religion.

3.pericope_label: The idols are buried under the oak, and the terror of God covers the journey

schools.summary: Gill reads the setting out as the fruit of the purging just commanded: their tents clear of idols, their bodies washed with pure water and their garments clean, all symbolical of inward purity and of freedom from idolatry, as became those who go to the house of God. Calvin is less sanguine about the motive. Though the holy man had his house in suitable subordination, the promptness with which they cast their idols away persuades him that they were moved by the fear of danger; from which we may infer how important it is to be roused from slumber by suffering, superstition being pertinacious and rebellious. He objects to the burial itself: it seems absurd that Jacob should have buried the idols under an oak rather than broken them and consumed them in the fire, as Moses did the golden calf and Hezekiah the brazen serpent, and the fact is not related without reason, but touches the infirmity of Jacob, who had not been provident enough against the future. Yet God accepted the obedience, defective as it was, knowing the holy man meant to remove the idols and, in token of his detestation, to bury them. On the terror that covered the retreat Calvin makes it the proof that the promise was not given in vain, since amid so many hostile swords Jacob goes forth not only safe but undisturbed: by the destruction of the Shechemites all the neighbouring people were inflamed against a single family, yet no one moves to take vengeance, from which we learn that the hearts of men are in the hand of God, who can inspire with fortitude those who in themselves are weak, and soften their iron hardness whenever he pleases. Whenever we see the wicked bent on our destruction, he says, lest our hearts fail and be broken by desperation, let us call to mind this terror of God, by which the rage of the whole world may easily be subdued.

Clarke fixes the day of distress more exactly than the words do: not only the flight from Esau, but more particularly the greatest strait of all, at the brook Jabbok. Of the earrings he holds that whether the rings were in the ears of the gods or in those of Jacob's family, they were certainly not mere ornaments but served superstitious purposes, being worn as amulets and charms, first consecrated to some god or formed under some constellation, with magical characters and images drawn upon them. Of the terror he says it was a supernatural awe sent by the Almighty upon the cities round about, so that they were not molested in their departure — owing, he says, to nothing less than the especial providence of God. Wesley reads the burial more favourably than Calvin: Jacob took care to bury the images in some place unknown to the household, that they might not afterwards find them and return to them; and of the terror he draws the plainer moral, that God governs the world more by secret terrors on men's minds than we are aware of.

Ellicott looks at the effect on the hearers: the narrative of Jacob's life and the detail of God's care of him would strongly affect his followers and make them ready to abandon their idols and worship the God that was Israel's God. He agrees with Clarke that the earrings were superstitious rather than ornamental and adds the telling parallel, that it was from their earrings that Aaron made the golden calf. On the tree he is precise: not Abraham's oak-grove, but the tree under which Joshua set up his pillar of witness, the word in both places being that for a terebinth. The terror he takes as a Hebrew idiom, a terror of God meaning simply a very great terror, granting that to the deeply religious Hebrew mind everything great and wonderful was the direct working of the Deity.

6.pericope_label: The altar El-bethel is built, and Deborah is buried under the oak of weeping

schools.summary: Gill locates the place first: the Bethel Jacob had named was formerly Luz, and is called here in the land of Canaan to distinguish it from the other Luz in the land of the Hittites. On Deborah he weighs and rejects the rabbinic account, from Jarchi, that Rebekah sent her to fetch Jacob home according to her promise, thinking it not probable that she should send a woman so ancient on such an errand, and preferring that the nurse returned to Haran after a stay in Canaan. Calvin says the fathers built their own altars to make it manifest that they did not worship gods of various kinds, as the world then did, but had a God peculiar to themselves; and that whereas others built rashly to unknown gods, Jacob adhered to the word, there being no lawful altar but what the word consecrates. He then defends the doubled divine name against the charge of over-familiarity: the title commends the faith of the holy man, since he confines himself within the bounds God prescribed, and as God, when he descends to us, in a certain sense abases himself and stammers with us, so he allows us to stammer with him. On the grammar he parts from the others, since the word for God is plural: he interprets it of the angels who had appeared on the ladder, holding that Jacob beheld the glory of God in the angels as we see the splendour of the sun through his rays. Of Deborah he has nothing certain to affirm, except that perhaps she had loved Jacob from a boy because she had nursed him, and knowing the cause of his exile followed him out of regard for religion.

Henry and Wesley take the altar together: Jacob built it and no doubt offered sacrifice upon it, perhaps the tenth of his cattle according to his vow, and he called the altar, not the place, El-bethel — as when he acknowledged the honour of being called Israel he worshipped God by the name El-elohe-Israel, so now, recognising the former favour shown him here, he worships him as the God of Bethel. Henry adds the application: the comfort the saints have in holy ordinances is not so much from Bethel, the house of God, as from El-bethel, the God of the house. On Deborah he supposes that Jacob, while his family dwelt near Shechem, went often to visit his father at Hebron; Rebekah was probably dead by then, but her old nurse survived her, and Jacob took her into his family to be a companion to his wives, her countrywomen, and an instructor to his children. He draws the moral that old servants who have been faithful ought to be respected, and that family afflictions may come even when family reformation is on foot — therefore rejoice with trembling.

Clarke reads the name El-bethel as the strong God, the house of the strong God, but reports that the first El is wanting in one of De Rossi's manuscripts and in the Septuagint, Vulgate, Syriac and some copies of the Arabic, and judges that the sentence reads much better without it and more consistently with the parallel passages. On Deborah he denies the premise the others argue from: the text does not state that she was in Jacob's family at all, her death being mentioned merely because his household had now arrived at the place where she was buried. He notes that Virgil mentions the nurse of Aeneas in nearly the same way.

Ellicott notes the plural verb — contrary to rule, though the Samaritan Pentateuch has the singular — but takes it for the ordinary Hebrew idiom, since in no other language is the name of God plural while its verbs are singular. On Deborah he reasons from her whereabouts: she was at Hebron with Rebekah when Jacob set out for Haran, so he must have gone thither before this and seen his father.

9.pericope_label: God appears again, confirms the name Israel, and Jacob sets up the pillar

schools.summary: Calvin denies that the first name is abolished by the second. Jacob was so called from the womb because he had wrestled with his brother, and Israel afterwards because he contended with God and obtained the victory — not that he prevailed by his own power, having borrowed courage and strength and arms from God alone, but because it was the Lord's will freely to confer the honour; the words are comparative, and the older and obscurer name gives place to the more splendid. Of the promise of a congregation of nations he finds the phrase the hardest in the oracle, since taken of natural descent it would be a curse rather than a blessing, the safety of the Church depending on its unity. On the pillar he subscribes to those who take the reference to be to what had been done before, Jacob having come not to dwell there but that a fresh view of the place might renew his faith in the ancient oracle. Gill reads the going up as from above him, a visible appearance of the glory of the Lord, or as the Targums say of the Shechinah, even of the Son of God in human form, ascending till he disappeared; and he thinks the pillar a new one, since the old had stood thirty years and was likely demolished by the heathen or fallen to ruin, though some render the words had set up.

Clarke is emphatic that the going up was no vision: this was not a strong mental impression but a real manifestation of God, whom Jacob saw and heard speak and before whose eyes he ascended to heaven — no doubt the future Saviour, the Angel of the covenant. On the pillar he supposes it probably the same one, thrown down since and now consecrated afresh. Wesley reads the ratification practically: what the wrestling angel had done was here confirmed by the divine majesty to encourage him against the fear of the Canaanites — for who can be too hard for Israel, a prince with God? On the pillar he splits the difference between the others: Jacob had formerly set up the stone he slept on, but now erected one more stately and durable, probably inserting that stone into it. With Ellicott he ends on the irony of the name, that with so grand a beginning the town was debased to unholy uses and became Bethaven, the house of iniquity, where Jeroboam set up one of his calves — it being impossible, Wesley says, for the best of men to entail so much as the form of religion upon a place.

Keil sets the second appearing against the first: God appeared again once the vow was performed and the altar built, as he had thirty years before on the journey thither, but then in a dream and now by daylight in a visible form, the gloom of that day of fear having brightened into the clear daylight of salvation. The appearance was God's answer to Jacob's acknowledgement of him, and Keil urges its reality against the conjecture that it is a legendary repetition of the earlier vision. Ellicott corrects the rendering: the word out is not in the Hebrew, which says on his coming from Padan-aram, that is, on his arrival at Bethel, and the insertion leads to confusion with the revelation of the earlier chapter; at Bethel going forth Jacob had seen the dream that assured him of protection, and at Bethel returning God renews the covenant, confirms the name Israel and transfers to him the promises. He identifies El-shaddai as the name under which God entered into covenant with Abraham, and renders the promise a congregation of nations. Of the going up he notes that the formula marks this manifestation as more solemn than any previous one, being in fact the acknowledgment of the patriarch as heir of the Abrahamic covenant.

16.pericope_label: Rachel dies in travail on the road to Ephrath and is buried under a pillar

schools.summary: Calvin asks why the loss fell here, and answers that the Lord intended to correct the exorbitance of Jacob's affection. The Holy Spirit fixes no mark of infamy upon Leah, a holy woman endowed with the greater virtue, but Jacob more highly appreciated Rachel's beauty; the fault was cured by a bitter medicine when his wife was taken from him, for the Lord often deprives the faithful of his gifts to correct their perverse abuse of them. From the refusal of the midwife's comfort he infers how far gone she was: the ancients were very desirous of offspring, especially male, and since Rachel does not accept this consolation we may conclude that she was completely oppressed with pain, and died in agonies, thinking of nothing but her sad childbirth. On the two names he thinks Jacob was correcting an error, since the change shows that in his judgment his wife's excess of sorrow was wrong, she having branded his son with a sinister and opprobrious name. Of the monument he says the fathers could not have attended to burial with such care but for their hope of the resurrection; Jacob reared no citadel as a token of his glory, but a sepulchre, to witness to all ages that he was the more devoted to the life to come. Gill draws from the departing soul that death is the disunion of soul and body, the soul not dying with it but going into a world of spirits, even unto God who gave it.

Henry tells the travail with Wesley: she fell in labour by the way, unable to reach the next town though they were near it, so suddenly does pain come upon a woman in travail; and her labour was harder than usual, which Henry takes for the effect of the ancient sentence — human life begins with sorrow, and the roses of its joy are set about with thorns. The midwife had her word ready, since Rachel at Joseph's birth had said God would add another son, and now tells her that her words were made good; yet this did not keep up her spirits, for unless God command away fear no one else can, and he only says it as one having authority. Henry reads the timing of the whole affliction as a check: great afflictions sometimes befall us immediately after great comforts, and lest Jacob be lifted up with the visions of the Almighty this was sent as a thorn in the flesh. With Wesley he sets the two pillars side by side — one raised in remembrance of his joys and this in remembrance of his sorrows.

Clarke says the term translated a little way has greatly perplexed commentators; it occurs only in this book and once in Kings, and seems some measure applied to land as we say a mile or a rood, but the exact quantity cannot be ascertained. On the departing soul he asks whether this is not a proof of an immortal spirit in man that can exist independent of the body: it is said of Rachel that her soul went away, and her body did not, so that soul and body must be distinct; had breath only been intended, another word would have served. Wesley joins Henry throughout the travail and the pillars.

Ellicott counts a fourth occurrence of the disputed word, in Amos, where it means a sieve, whence many of the Rabbins translate in the spring-time, the earth being then riddled by the plough; the real meaning, he concludes, is lost. Of the name Ben-oni he grants the word has a double meaning and is rendered strength elsewhere, but doubts not her feeling was that her offspring's life had been purchased by her own death. Keil looks ahead to the next stage, beyond Migdal Eder, the flock-tower built to protect flocks against robbers.

21.pericope_label: Reuben defiles his father's bed, and the twelve sons are numbered

schools.summary: Gill observes that this is the first time Moses calls him Israel since the name was given, and reports the Jewish reason, that he had borne Rachel's death with so much patience. Calvin weighs the offence more heavily than the rest. Though Moses calls Bilhah a concubine, as it respected the bed she was Jacob's lawful wife; and if a stranger had defiled the wife of the holy man it would have been a great disgrace, but far more atrocious that he should suffer such an indignity from his own son. On the silence about Jacob's grief he offers a comparison: Moses conceals it not because the patriarch was unfeeling but because his grief was too great to be expressed, as the painter who, representing the sacrifice of Iphigenia, veiled the father's face, being unable to show its sorrow. He then turns the story against a later error, that Reuben after this extreme act of iniquity still retained his rank of a patriarch in the Church, so that the Novatians have no right to cut off the hope of pardon from the lapsed.

Henry takes the name as an honour deliberately given: Jacob sojourned in the land of promise as in a strange country, and the historian calls him Israel here because he bore that affliction with such submission to Providence — for those are Israels indeed, princes with God, who support the government of their own passions. On the crime he and Wesley take it as it stands, a piece of abominable wickedness, that very sin which the apostle says is not so much as named among the Gentiles; they note that it happened when Israel dwelt in that land, as if he were absent from his family, which might be the unhappy occasion of it, and that though Bilhah was perhaps the greater criminal, Reuben's crime cost him his birthright. Of the father they say only what the text says: Israel heard it, and no more is added, which is enough — he heard it with the utmost grief and shame, horror and displeasure.

Clarke alone looks for a mitigation. Jonathan in his Targum says that Reuben only overthrew the bed of Bilhah, set up opposite his mother Leah's, and that this was reputed to him as if he had lain with her, the colouring being that he was incensed to find Bilhah preferred after Rachel's death to his own mother; could that view be proved, Clarke says, both piety and candour would rejoice. On the tower he takes it literally as the tower of the flock, built by shepherds near a well, supposes it about a mile from Bethlehem, and reports the tradition that it was where the angels appeared to the shepherds, the Targum of Jonathan calling it the place where the King Messiah shall be manifested in the end of days. Wesley adds the other half of Henry's contrast: Israel, a prince with God, yet dwells in tents, the city being reserved for the other world.

Ellicott looks north for the tower: Micah calls it the hill of the daughter of Zion, and the word there often means a beacon-hill on which a watch-tower is raised, so it may have stood a few miles south of Jerusalem. He takes the meaning to be that Jacob now occupied the whole region permanently with his cattle — until Esau withdrew to Seir there was no room for his flocks at Hebron, but at Eder he was near enough to visit his father often, so that his exile was over and he was at last at home. With Clarke he notes that the Hebrew breaks off in mid-verse, the Masora marking a hiatus which the Septuagint fills with the words, it appeared evil in his sight. Keil explains why the list of sons stands where it does: Jacob had left his father's house with no possession but a staff and returned with twelve sons, so the account of his arrival at Hebron is preceded by the roll of them, arranged by their mothers and closed with the remark that they were born in Padan-aram, though Benjamin was born on the journey back.

23.pericope_label: The sons of Jacob listed, and Isaac dies and is buried by Esau and Jacob

schools.summary: Gill infers from the silence about his mother that Rebekah was dead, and supposes that Isaac, alone and very old, may have sent for Jacob to come with his family. In the joint burial he sees the proof that the reconciliation between the brothers was real and had continued. Calvin says the death is not related in its proper order, being mentioned here to prevent a later interruption of the history, and that the events of the two following chapters came first, Isaac having lived some fifteen years after Joseph was carried into Egypt. He will not let the phrase full of days pass as a formula: it means that Isaac, having fulfilled the course of his life, departed by a mature death, to be ascribed to the blessing of God; but he refers the words not merely to the duration of the life but to the state of the feelings, implying that Isaac, satisfied with life, willingly and placidly departed out of the world. For we may see decrepit old men, he says, not less desirous of life than in the flower of their age, who with one foot in the grave still have a horror of death; so it is not enough to count up many years unless a man feels he has lived long and, satisfied with the favour of God, prepares for his departure. That Esau is named first he takes for a lesson, that the fruit of the paternal benediction was not received by Jacob in this life, since he who was first-born by right is still put after the other even after their father's death.

Clarke opens the roll by observing that the children are arranged under their mothers and not in the order of their birth, and glosses the closing formula: born to him in Padan-aram means all but Benjamin, who was born in Canaan; and Padan-aram is Mesopotamia, a word signifying between the two rivers. He reports as generally allowed that the death is anticipated here so that the history of Joseph might not be disturbed, and reckons the interval at twelve years at least. Wesley notes that Isaac, a mild quiet man, lived the longest of all the patriarchs, and makes the funeral the point of the whole: particular notice is taken of the amicable agreement of the brothers in solemnising it, to show how wonderfully God had changed Esau's mind since he vowed his brother's murder against the day of his father's death — for God has many ways of preventing ill men from the mischief they intended, and can either tie their hands or turn their hearts.

Ellicott says the closing formula is to be taken generally, since Benjamin was born in Canaan. That Esau is named first he takes for simple precedence: Esau apparently still dwelt at Hebron until his father died and here takes his place as the elder by natural right, but having learnt the advantages of Seir and how little the Horites could resist him, he gives up Hebron to his brother and migrates thither with his wealth. Keil explains what the arrival at Mamre meant: Jacob's coming to the terebinth-grove by Kirjath-arba was his entrance into his father's house, to remain there as Isaac's heir. He had probably visited during the ten years since his return, though no allusion is made to it, such visits having no importance for the sacred history — which was not the case with this return to enter upon the family inheritance, and with it the history of Isaac's life is closed.
